Project isolation

Confidential and sealed projects - what each state promises, how tightening works, and the limits of the fence.

By default, projects are cooperative rather than isolated. Any agent can read or write any project by passing project, global memories reach every briefing, and family surfaces deliberately carry knowledge between related projects. That is the right default for one person's interlocking work.

It is the wrong default for a client project, private research, or anything you need to keep out of the agents serving your other work. Isolation is the per-project setting that draws a real boundary.

The three states

Isolation is directional. The two fenced states solve different problems and should not be conflated.

State Nothing leaves Nothing enters
open (default) no no
confidential yes no
sealed yes yes

open shares normally. Global knowledge flows in; family surfaces may include it.

confidential - nothing leaves. Sessions bound elsewhere can never read this project: not by explicit project=, not by ULID, not through trials, not through recall. It is excluded from family surfaces and from the gardener's cross-project passes. Critically, sessions bound to it cannot write outside it - not to another slug, and not to project: global, because an agent-initiated global write is a leak too.

Inbound is deliberately unchanged: its agents still receive your global memories and can still read open projects. This is the common case - sensitive work that still wants your conventions available inside it.

sealed - nothing in or out. Confidential plus the inbound fence. Briefing, recall, and the prompt matcher scope to the project alone; global memories are dropped, there is no family, and there are no cross-project reads in either direction. A clean room.

Because a sealed project's world is genuinely smaller, its agents are told so. The briefing carries a line stating the mode, on both the main and subagent surfaces, so an agent inside understands why a write outside will be refused rather than discovering it as an unexplained error.

Isolation is about what flows in and out of a project. Whether even the project's own agents need a fresh approval from you first is a second setting, the lock, and "locked" never means sealed. A sensitive project is normally confidential and locked: Lock projects behind your approval says when to use which.

The console is exempt

The threat model is agent-to-agent leakage, not hiding from you. Console search and views still see everything; isolated projects are simply badged with a lock pill. Nothing about an isolated project's pages turns scary or half-rendered - the pill and the Overview control are the whole story.

The one exception is a locked project under peer_auth: there the threat is your own account, so the console shows its name and counts, and nothing inside it until you unlock it in that browser. A session's Conversation card follows the same rule: a locked project in it shows its name and nothing more.

Isolation requires a standalone project

A project cannot be isolated while it is entangled in a family: no family membership, no parent, no children.

Tightening therefore detaches family membership and the parent link, and the confirmation step shows you exactly which. A project with children refuses to tighten until they are re-parented - Seamless will not silently orphan a scope that inherits from it.

This keeps the fence surface small. Rather than threading isolation checks through every topology path, the rule guarantees there is no topology to thread. The briefing-side exclusions remain anyway, as defense in depth against stale data.

Tightening and loosening

Tightening is the ceremonious direction, because it changes what other agents can see. It is two-step in the console: choosing confidential or sealed returns a confirmation panel stating exactly what will change - the family and parent it will detach from, or the children blocking it, plus the promise of the state you picked - and applies only when you confirm.

Loosening is immediate. It is fully reversible and nothing leaked while the fence was up, so there is nothing to confirm.

Knowledge that already got out

Raising a fence does nothing about what escaped before it existed. The most likely leak is global memories written by this project's own sessions - they were the right call at the time and are now injected into every other project's briefing, forever.

So tightening runs a provenance audit: it traces global memories back through source_session to the sessions that wrote them, and for each one that belonged to this project it files a relocate proposal in the Gardener inbox offering to move it behind the fence.

Two things this deliberately is not. It does not move anything on its own - the gardener only ever proposes, and dismissing the proposal is how you say the memory really is general knowledge. And it does not run on a timer: once the fence is up, the write funnel refuses this project's sessions any write outside it, so the leak set is closed at the moment of tightening and never grows.

The confirmation step tells you the count before you commit, and distinguishes a proven zero from an unanswered question - if the audit could not run, it says nothing rather than reporting "none".

In the console

The control lives on the project's Overview tab: a three-option segmented control with each state's promise written under it. The isolation change is recorded as an event, so it appears in Recent activity like any other change.

From the CLI

seam project isolation <slug>                    # print the current state and its promise
seam project isolation <slug> confidential       # print consequences, apply nothing
seam project isolation <slug> confidential --yes # apply
seam project isolation <slug> open               # loosen, immediate

Tightening requires --yes, which stands in for the console's confirmation step: without it the command prints the same consequences and exits having changed nothing.

What agents see

  • project_list reports each project's isolation state, so an agent can discover the boundary rather than guess at it.
  • project_create accepts isolation. There is no tool to change it afterwards: tightening detaches topology and is an owner decision, not an agent one.
  • Refusals state the rule and the remedy and never echo the content they are withholding - an error that quoted the memory it was protecting would leak the very thing the fence exists to keep in. They do not hide that the project exists, because every scope error already lists the machine's projects. An outside agent refused at the fence is told to bind to the project with session_start project=<slug> if its task really is that project, and to leave it alone otherwise. With access requests on, a Claude Code or Codex agent is told instead to ask you to move its conversation into the project, or for a grant of it, and the refusal names the request it filed.
  • A conversation that binds itself in keeps its record inside. A Claude Code or Codex agent working in an open project's repository (or in none) that binds itself to a confidential or sealed project with session_start project=<slug> records its SessionEnd harvest (for Codex, each Stop's findings), its plan captures and its planning-subagent reports in that project, under the session session_start opened there, with their events - for the rest of the conversation, wherever it binds afterwards. The session it left in the open project ends with a pointer naming the project and nothing it holds. One that binds itself to two isolated projects keeps that record in none of them. A confidential or sealed project's own agent keeps its record at home, whatever it binds itself to. This holds on every install, whether or not isolation.requests is on (details). With isolation.requests on, everything the hooks record follows the conversation's home instead, wherever the agent works, and nothing lands where the clearance refuses (details).
  • Task answers withhold what blocks across the fence. A confidential project's task that blocks an outside project's task reaches an outside session as a withheld entry in tasks_ready, a depends_on_withheld count in place of its id, and a count in the claim's "task blocked" refusal - never its title or its id.

What a security monitor sees

A monitor you feed from Seamless follows a fenced project without learning its name: the metadata feed sends a confidential or sealed project's slug only as a keyed hash, and the commit-matching snapshot never names its repository. Both are off by default.

Asking for access: one home per conversation

A refusal at a confidential or sealed project's fence can become a request you approve, when the daemon's config turns it on (isolation.requests: true; see the configuration). It is off by default, and off every refusal reads exactly as above and nothing is recorded.

Isolation itself is unchanged by it: a confidential project's own sessions still read open projects and global, and nothing leaves a fenced project without your approval. What changes is who the fence judges. Without the switch it judges the session a connection is bound to, which an agent can change at will (session_start, session=). With it, the fence judges the conversation, and what a conversation has read only grows.

The conversation, its home and its label

  • The conversation is one agent context. Without peer_auth it is the client's own session - the Claude Code or Codex session id that the agent-process identity on every call names (how) - so session_start, session= and a move leave it the same conversation; a resume continues it, and /clear starts a new one. Under peer_auth it is the agent's process tree as the kernel reports it, for the life of the process, /clear included.
  • Its home is the project its own session is in: the repository's project when the agent starts, and after an approved move the project it moved into. Its own record goes there, and calls that name no project work there. The home does not limit what the conversation may reach.
  • Its label is every confidential or sealed project whose content it may hold: a fenced home, every project a grant opened to it, every project it moved through, and every fenced project one of its own sessions is in. The label only grows: a grant's expiry or revocation ends the reads, never what was read. A project you loosen to open leaves every label.

A Claude Code or Codex agent running the hooks with a current seam is identified this way, from its own session. A client that sends no agent-process identity is not: it is held by the session it is bound to, and binds exactly as it did before.

The one rule

Every write must be cleared for everything the conversation holds. A destination is cleared when every project in the label is that destination or has a flow into it: your approval, recorded with the request that listed it, for one project's content to be written into another. An open project and the global scope are cleared only while the label is empty.

So a conversation that holds nothing fenced writes wherever it always could. One that holds example-finance's content writes only where you let that content go, and never again into an open project or the global scope - its own open home included. A confidential or sealed project's own conversation writes into it as before. The rule lives in the fence itself, so every tool, every hook and every other agent write meets it, and a refusal names the projects the conversation holds and where it may still write:

memory_write: this session holds content from example-finance, example-legal, so it writes only into example-legal: a write into project example-hr is refused

What a refused call asks for

The kind of request follows from the conversation's home and the project, never from the agent's choice:

The conversation's home The project it reaches The request
open, or the global scope confidential a move into the project
confidential another confidential project a grant of the project
any sealed a move into the project
sealed confidential none: a sealed project's conversation reaches no confidential project

An open project needs no request. A conversation that holds fenced content never goes back to one, so a write there, or a session_start there, is refused, and nothing is filed.

What files one:

  • A refused read - naming the project with project= (in recall or any other read), or reading one of its items by ULID. A read that only filters, such as recall without project= or trial_query, asks for nothing.
  • A refused write, which asks for read and write.
  • session_start project=<slug> into a fenced project, which binds nothing, asks for read and write, and leaves the home where it is. A session= handle naming another project's session acts as that session only where the home may read and write; anywhere else the call is refused, and nothing is filed.
  • The agent's explicit ask: access_request (with write to ask for read and write) or, from its own shell, seam access request example-finance --reason "..." [--write].

The refusal names the request it filed. Here a conversation working in example-ops, an open project, reads one of example-finance's items by id:

notes_read: project example-finance is confidential: only a conversation working in it reads it -- if your task is about example-finance, ask the owner to move this conversation into it (session_start project=example-finance asks); otherwise leave it alone
Remedy: move request R-7F3K is waiting -- the owner approves it in their own terminal with `seam approve R-7F3K`, or with Approve on the console's Access requests page; retry once it is approved. Record what belongs in example-ops now: once the owner approves the move, this conversation works in example-finance for good, and it can no longer write to example-ops or the global scope until the conversation ends. After the move it can still close a task it claimed there, with a receipt: tasks_update with status done or dropped, and no text. Its first result after the approval says so and carries example-finance's briefing.

A locked project stays the lock's: a call refused at the lock files the lock's request, as without the switch. An agent working elsewhere that needs to work in a locked project asks with access_request write=true (or seam access request <project> --write), which files the move or the grant its home calls for; approving that opens the lock to it too. A lease alone opens a locked project only to the conversation that works in it (details).

Asking again. One request waits per conversation and project, whatever its kind: a repeated refusal names the request already waiting rather than filing another, and an explicit ask with a reason fills in the reason of a waiting request that has none (a refusal never has one to give). That reason is one of the facts you approve, so if you were looking at the request when it arrived, the approval asks you to look again. A conversation that already holds a live grant of the project, with at least the access it asks for, is answered with it, and nothing is filed, until 30 minutes before it ends; from then on asking again files a new request.

After you deny one. The agent's next refused call for that project says you denied it, and when, and files nothing: a refused call never asks you again behind your back. If you denied it because it asked for the wrong thing, tell the agent what to ask for instead; its explicit request always files a new one.

What you approve

Every request states the whole carry: the conversation's home, every fenced project it would hold once approved, and every project it could write to then. Approving clears exactly the flows those facts list. seam approve, each request's page on the console (its passkey page under peer_auth) and the advisory tier's in-session dialog show it, and every surface shows the line that says what approving lets happen among the warnings:

  • A move: This agent has worked in example-ops and read example-legal. If you approve, it works in example-finance from now on, and what it saw may be written into example-finance. It can no longer write to example-ops or the global scope until the conversation ends. Into a sealed project the line adds that the project is sealed, so nothing enters it otherwise, and that approving lets in what the agent carries.
  • A grant: content from example-finance may be copied into example-legal, and into every other project the conversation may write to. Between confidential projects you choose read-only (the default) or read and write, which adds and it may change example-finance's tasks, memories and notes; content from example-legal may be copied into example-finance.

A grant lasts as long as you choose: until the conversation's session ends, 1 hour or 4 hours, capped by peer_auth.max_lease (8 hours when unset). A move lasts for good; into a locked project, the lock it opens lasts as long as you choose.

Moves

An approved move takes the conversation into the project for good:

  • the session it worked in ends, keeps the findings the agent wrote, and gains a pointer: Moved to project example-finance; this conversation continues there as session cc/8dd2fd5b-55d96b8d15ff0104@example-finance, and its findings go there, not here. Its task claims stay, for receipts;
  • a child session opens in the project, linked to it, and becomes the conversation's own session, with the same client session and agent process;
  • that project is the conversation's home from then on: its record goes there, and calls that name no project work there;
  • it can no longer write to the home it left, or to the global scope, until the conversation ends (under peer_auth, until the agent process exits);
  • its first tool result after the approval says so and carries the new home's briefing, once, even across a daemon restart. When it moved out of a confidential or sealed project, that notice also says where what it writes about that project goes: into its new home, by reference.

Before the move, the request tells the agent to record what belongs in its current home first. Moving in is the only way into a sealed project, and it is how an open project's conversation reaches a confidential one. A resumed conversation resumes in the project it moved into (details).

Grants: read-only, or read and write

A grant opens one confidential project to a conversation working in another confidential project. Read-only, the conversation reads the project, and what it reads may be written only into the projects the approval names: its home, and any project it already holds a read-and-write grant of. Read and write, it also changes the project's tasks, memories and notes as the project's own sessions do, and what it holds may be written into it. Nothing that involves a sealed project is ever granted, on either side.

While a grant lives, the project also joins the conversation's recall scope, its trials show in trial_query, its proposals show in gardener_proposals, and prompt recall and a subagent's relevant memories read it; the briefing does not change. A grant ends at its expiry, when you revoke it from the Access requests page, or when the conversation's session ends. Ending it ends the reads, never what the conversation holds.

The grant tells the agent to write up its work in its home and to refer to the project's items by reference, leaving its confidential details out. That is an instruction to the agent, not a filter, which is why the line you approve still says content may be copied.

Receipts

A move is one way: once you approve it, the conversation can no longer write into the project it left. One write is still allowed there, because without it the work it claimed before the move would stay in progress for good: a receipt. The conversation closes a task its pre-move session claimed - done or dropped, nothing else - and may point at one item in its new home (reference=example-finance:<id>, the project slug and the item's id). That is the only thing that crosses back: a receipt carries no title, body or other text, and Seamless refuses one that tries, or whose reference names no item in the home. The typical case is an orchestrator in an open project that claims a build step, then moves to read a confidential project's live data: the receipt closes the step without carrying any of that data back. The task's history shows the receipt and its reference under the session that claimed the step. A conversation whose home is sealed sends no receipts, and a task someone else has claimed since, or one you released from the console, is no receipt's to close. The move's request and its notice both tell the agent so.

Where the conversation's record goes

With the switch on, everything the hooks record for a conversation goes to its home, wherever the agent works: the SessionEnd harvest (for Codex, each Stop's findings), plan captures and planning-subagent reports, and the events about them. After a move that is the project it moved into. Prompt recall and a subagent's briefing read the home and the projects its live grants open. Where the rule refuses the home - an open home holding fenced content - nothing is recorded, and the session's findings say why (details).

Provenance stamps

Everything an agent writes while it holds content from a confidential or sealed project other than the destination records may contain content from example-finance (grant R-7F3K): one stamp per such project, naming the grant or move that let its content in. That covers memories, notes, tasks, trials, session findings, and plan and subagent captures. Memories and notes keep it in frontmatter (may_contain); the rest only in the database. No write removes it, and a memory that supersedes another carries both memories' stamps. It names projects and approvals, never content. It shows on recall hits, memory_read, notes_read, tasks_list and tasks_ready answers, and the console's item pages and search; on a project's page, Came from narrows its items to the ones that name a project (console). Deleting may_contain from a file by hand removes the warning. Off, nothing is stamped.

Source references

Where the agent writes follows one placement rule: the destination must be cleared first; then the project the item is about; and when that project is not cleared, the item goes in the conversation's home, citing what it came from by reference. A reference is body text in one form, the project slug, a colon and the item's full id - example-finance:01M7... - so no tool takes an argument for it. The grant's text, the refusals that send a conversation home and the notice after a move out of a fenced project teach that form.

The gardener reads references back from stamped memories, and never a source's content:

  • stale-copy proposes archiving a copy whose cited memory, note or task changed after the copy was last written;
  • copy-relocate proposes moving a copy whose stamps and references all name one other project into that project. Before you move a stamped memory into a project less fenced than one it may hold content from, the console warns you, and blocks nothing.

A reference that does not resolve in the project it names, or points into a project the copy may not read, is skipped.

How much an approval proves

Without peer_auth an approval is advisory. seam approve asks for a y/N in a terminal (it refuses to run without one) and commits over the console with the bearer key; the console's Approve does the same, and so does Approve in the agent's in-session dialog. Any process that holds the key - which every local agent can read - can make that call, so an approval guards against an agent wandering into a fenced project, not against one set on it. The conversation is the one the agent's process identity names, which is self-reported; a client that sends none is held by the session a call speaks for, so one that rebinds with session_start, or names another session with session=, writes where that session may.

Under peer_auth a grant or a move needs the same proofs as a locked project's lease: your terminal through sudo to the daemon's account, a passkey, or - for a grant - a Touch ID key; Touch ID approves no move yet. The conversation is then the asking agent's process tree, and a move or grant into a locked project opens its lock too, in the same approval.

In either tier, an agent whose conversation Seamless identifies cannot name a fenced project as its own: session_start files a move or grant request instead of binding, and session= acts as another project's session only where the home may read and write. A client that sends no identity still can, and so can an agent started in that project's repository, which is that project's own; only a lock holds against that.

Honest limits

This matters more than the feature list, so it is stated plainly.

What this is. A policy fence at every Seamless surface - briefings, recall, tool reads and writes, the gardener. That is where accidental cross-contamination actually happens, and it is now closed.

What this is not. It is not a defense against a local agent reading ~/.seamless/memory/<project>/*.md directly. Without peer_auth, A2A's recall names its scope in the request's metadata.project, and the fence does not judge it there: the bearer key can read a confidential project that way. Under peer_auth A2A speaks for no session, so it refuses a confidential or sealed project. Every MCP caller shares one static bearer key, and the fence keys off the self-reported session binding - an explicit session_start, or the agent-process identity a Claude Code or Codex agent's seam transport sends, which is just as self-reported (how it binds). That automatic binding is what lets a confidential project's own agents read it without a session_start, and what keeps a confidential or sealed project's agents from writing outside it. A connection bound to nothing - a hookless client that skipped session_start, or an older seam that sends no identity - is judged as the global scope, which fails closed against reading an isolated project but also means the fence cannot recognize it as belonging to one.

With access requests on, the same holds, and more:

  • Seamless guards its own surfaces only. An agent can still put what it read into files, commits, pull request text or another tool.
  • Without peer_auth the conversation is the agent's word: the agent-process identity is self-reported, and /clear starts a new conversation with an empty label. A client that sends no identity is held by its session, as before.
  • A fork, or a separate agent the conversation starts, is a new conversation to Seamless, and what it prints back is invisible to it.
  • The event log records each tool call under the calling session's project, with its arguments and the start of its result, so a granted read's answer can appear in the asking project's history on the console. Agents read no events, and text already in the log stays there.

What makes it stronger. peer_auth puts an authentication boundary under the fence: the daemon runs as its own OS account, names each caller by the uid the kernel reports for its Unix-socket connection, and lets you lock a project, so that even your own agents reach it only with an approval you prove, through a tool or through a file. Use it with isolation, not instead of it: a locked project must also be confidential or sealed.

Without it, the hard boundary is a separate Seamless instance - its own data dir, port, and key, run as its own account.
